headline: New Hampshire revenue surges on record September business-tax collections
dek: The state collected $398.9 million for its General and Education funds in September, beating the monthly plan by $69.1 million as quarterly business-tax payments arrived.
body: New Hampshire's General and Education funds received a major revenue lift in September, when the state collected $398.9 million in unrestricted receipts. The total was $69.1 million, or 21%, above the $329.8 million monthly plan, according to the [New Hampshire Department of Administrative Services monthly revenue report](https://www.das.nh.gov/accounting/FY%2027/FY2027_Monthly_Revenue_September.pdf). Gov. Kelly Ayotte highlighted the results in a [statement issued Oct. 5](https://www.governor.nh.gov/news/statement-september-revenues), saying the figures showed the state's economy was moving in the right direction.

The biggest factor was business-tax revenue. Collections from the Business Profits Tax and Business Enterprise Tax totaled $269.8 million in September, $69.4 million above the state's plan and $94.7 million higher than September 2025, the report says. The month's total also exceeded the previous September record of $226.4 million, set in 2024. The report attributes the increase to estimated payments, extension payments and returns, along with fewer refunds than a year earlier.

September is an important checkpoint because many businesses make quarterly estimated payments during the month. The New Hampshire Fiscal Policy Institute had warned in a September analysis that July and August offered only a limited view of the fiscal year because the state's largest revenue source, business-profit taxes, arrives unevenly. The institute said September would provide a stronger indication of whether early 2027 fiscal-year collections could help support the next state budget. The new report covers the third month of the fiscal year, which began July 1.

After three months, unrestricted receipts for the two funds were $74.9 million, or 12.5%, above the state's revenue plan, according to the governor's statement. That does not mean every part of the revenue picture is outperforming. The report shows the General Fund was $54 million ahead of plan and the Education Fund was $20.9 million ahead after the first quarter, but transfers from the Liquor Commission were $7.4 million below the first-quarter plan and video-lottery-terminal receipts were $3 million short.

Other sources also helped. Real-estate-transfer-tax collections reached $73.6 million in September, exceeding the plan by $8.3 million and the year-earlier total by $11.9 million. Meals-and-rentals-tax receipts, after transfers for municipal revenue and school-building debt service, totaled $111.8 million for the quarter, up $4.3 million from the same period last year. The first-quarter transfer to the municipal revenue fund reached $43.9 million, according to reporting by [NH Journal](https://nhjournal.com/gop-tax-cuts-record-receipts-nh-revenues-beat-projections/).

The numbers are likely to feed New Hampshire's continuing argument over tax rates and public spending. Republican officials have pointed to the business-tax receipts as evidence that earlier rate reductions did not prevent revenue growth. Democrats and other critics have argued that strong collections do not settle questions about whether the state is adequately funding schools, local services and other obligations. Those are political interpretations of the report, not findings in the revenue data itself.

The results also come with limits. The September report is a cash-basis fiscal update rather than a forecast of the full year, and one strong month cannot establish a long-term trend. Business-tax collections can vary with corporate profits, payment timing, refunds and economic conditions. New Hampshire's fiscal reports will therefore remain important as lawmakers and agencies watch whether the early surplus persists into months with different revenue patterns.

For now, the report gives state budget writers more room than they had at the start of the fiscal year: the General and Education funds are ahead of plan, while the state's largest monthly business-tax haul has offset weaker performance in several other streams. The next question is whether the surplus represents durable growth or a concentration of payments in one unusually strong quarter.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: New Hampshire September revenue beats plan on business taxes
seoDescription: New Hampshire's September General and Education fund receipts beat the plan by $69.1 million, led by record business-tax collections.
